title: ‘Anonymous’ is a test, not a checklist: Italy fines IQVIA 7 million euros
summary: Italy fined IQVIA 7 million euros for health data it called anonymous. Learn why HIPAA's checklist doesn't answer the GDPR's three-part test.
body_markdown:
## What the Italian Authority Decided


Italy’s data protection authority has fined IQVIA Solutions Italy 7 million euros over a health database that IQVIA claimed was anonymous. The[decision](https://gpdp.it/garante/doc.jsp?ID=10302112) (No. 710) is dated Sept. 23, 2026. The authority announced it on Oct. 2, and the[European Data Protection Board (EDPB) posted a summary](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/italian-dpa-fines-iqvia-eur-7-000-000-for-unlawful-processing-of-patients-health-data_en) on Oct. 9.


IQVIA checked many of the boxes on a standard HIPAA-style de-identification checklist. According to IQVIA’s account in the decision, the software that collected the data removed names, surnames and addresses, cut birth dates to the month, and had risk assessments conducted for re-identification. The authority still found the data was not anonymous. In effect, most patients lost their names but kept their detailed medical histories.


**If you can follow a patient over time, assume the data is not anonymous until you can show otherwise.**


## HIPAA’s List vs. the GDPR’s Test


If you work with U.S. health data, you know the drill. The safe harbor method under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) takes the form of a list: remove 18 types of identifiers (the last being a catch-all for any other unique identifying number, characteristic or code, with a narrow exception) and have no actual knowledge that what remains could identify someone. HIPAA’s second method, expert determination, functions as a test, more similar to the GDPR. A qualified expert must find that the risk of identifying anyone from the data is very small.


The EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has no list. The authority asks three questions, drawn from the Article 29 Working Party’s 2014 opinion and the EDPB’s draft anonymization guidelines (adopted July 7, 2026, open for comment until Oct. 30, 2026). Using reasonably available means, could anyone \[1\] single a person out, \[2\] link records to other data about that person, or \[3\] infer new facts about that person? If any answer is yes, more analysis is needed before the data can be called anonymous.


## Why the Data Was Not Anonymous


According to the authority, the database held health information on about 1 million patients of 800 general practitioners. This information was used for studies, some of them commissioned by pharmaceutical companies. Each patient carried a code which made it possible to follow the same person over time. The authority concluded that this code, in combination with a patient’s year of birth, sex, diagnoses, symptoms, prescriptions, examinations, vaccinations and location data, allowed individual patients to be singled out and, by reasonably available means, re-identified.


IQVIA’s risk assessments used k-anonymity, which hides a person among others who share the same details, such as age and location. The authority established that k-anonymity is not enough when other parts of the record, such as diagnoses and medication patterns over time, can single a person out. A checklist asks what you removed; the authority asked what could still be linked. Removing someone’s name tag does not help much if the same person shows up to every appointment, revealing the telling fingerprint of a long medical history.


## The “We Are Only the Recipient” Argument


IQVIA argued that, from its own position, the data was anonymous: the key linking codes to patients sat in the doctors’ software, which it could not access. It relied on the EU Court of Justice’s judgment of Sept. 4, 2025 (case C-413/23 P, known as SRB), which, as the decision describes it, allows pseudonymized data to be non-personal for a recipient who cannot re-identify the people.


The authority did not reject the principle that pseudonymized data could be non-personal for a recipient of that sort. However, it found that IQVIA was not an ordinary recipient: it was the controller from the point of collection, because its contracts and instructions shaped the anonymization process. IQVIA was thus judged by what it could do, not by what it intended. Because, as the controller, it could re-identify patients by reasonable means, the data was personal for IQVIA.


## What Else the Authority Found


The usual GDPR duties accompany personal health data. The authority treated IQVIA as the controller and found that it had:


- no suitable legal basis, and no adequate information for patients
- no retention periods; the data went back as far as 2001
- no completed data protection impact assessment (DPIA)
- inadequate security: identifying details of about 3,370 patients, with health data for about 3,080, arrived through free-text fields


IQVIA says it uses pseudonymization and encryption. Both are good security measures, but neither turns personal data into anonymous data.


## What the Authority Ordered


Besides the fine, the authority gave IQVIA a few pathways. To keep processing, it had to, within 120 days of notification, take these steps and report back to the authority: find a legal basis, inform patients, carry out a DPIA and appoint the doctors as processors. Otherwise, the doctors could anonymize the data themselves, under safeguards specified by the authority.


In its penalty decision, the authority took into account the number of patients and the sensitivity of the data. In IQVIA’s favor, the general practitioners had stopped sending data and IQVIA cooperated during the proceedings.


That said, this is the decision of a single national authority, so other EU data protection agencies are not bound by it. IQVIA says it cooperated with the authority, has taken the necessary measures to comply with its orders and does not use the dataset in its clinical research services. The company has reserved the right to appeal.


## What This Means for GCs, CISOs and Founders


This matters most if you handle the personal data of people in the EU, because the GDPR may then apply to you. If you do not, the decision is still a useful test of what ‘anonymous’ should mean.


**General counsel.** ‘Anonymous’ in a contract is a statement of fact, and your name is on it. Calling yourself the recipient may not help if you shaped the process. An old assessment also may not survive a new ruling on a similar dataset. Check the controller and processor roles in your contracts too. If IQVIA continued processing the data, the authority wanted the doctors appointed as processors.


**CISOs.** Encryption and pseudonymization protect data but do not make it anonymous. The authority said hashing the patient ID does not prevent singling out. For security teams, the lesson concerns free-text fields. The authority faulted IQVIA for not checking, before or after collection, whether free-text fields were left out, and noted that such fields carry high risk.


**Founders.** If your product shares or sells ‘de-identified’ patient or user data, the claim that the data is de-identified is likely sitting in your pitch deck, your data-license terms and your privacy notice. All three should describe the data accurately and consistently. Regulators may test that claim, like Italy’s did.


U.S. companies accustomed to HIPAA ought to unlearn the checklist. A U.S. de-identification label does not answer the GDPR question, because the two systems set different standards.


## Action Items


1. **List every dataset you call anonymous or de-identified.** Take note of identifiers and persistent codes. Our post on[finding where personal data lives](https://general.legal/blog/dsar-data-mapping) may help with the inventory.
2. **Ask the three questions.** Using reasonably available means, could anyone \[1\] single out a person, \[2\] link records to other data about that person, or \[3\] infer new facts about them? If any answer is yes, assume the data is personal until an analysis shows otherwise.
3. **Check the free text.** Find every free-text field that feeds a dataset you call anonymous, and test it for names, ID or phone numbers and addresses. Free-text boxes collect surprising things. As IQVIA’s case shows, people often type identifying details into them.
4. **Check your roles and documents.** Make sure contracts, decks and privacy notices describe your data accurately, and that controller and processor roles match what really happens.


These steps serve as a first pass. Whether a real dataset holds up is a judgment call. The contract language and the documentation also have to survive a regulator’s questions. Key takeaways


- •


Italy's data protection authority fined IQVIA 7 million euros for processing health data it claimed was anonymous but which actually allowed individual patients to be singled out and re-identified.


- •


Under GDPR, anonymization is a three-part test—can anyone single out, link, or infer facts about a person—not a checklist of removed identifiers like HIPAA's safe harbor method.


- •


Removing direct identifiers while keeping longitudinal medical histories with persistent patient codes does not make data anonymous under EU law.


- •


IQVIA's argument that it was merely a recipient without re-identification capability failed because it controlled the anonymization process from the start.


- •


Free-text fields in the database leaked identifying details for over 3,000 patients, highlighting a common security gap in supposedly de-identified datasets.


- •


The decision makes clear that encryption and pseudonymization are security measures, not anonymization techniques, and k-anonymity alone is insufficient when detailed medical histories remain linkable.


TL;DR


The Fine and Finding Italy fined IQVIA €7M for processing a health database of 1 million patients that IQVIA called anonymous but which allowed individual re-identification through persistent codes and detailed medical histories.


GDPR's Three-Question Test GDPR asks whether anyone could single out, link, or infer facts about a person using reasonably available means—not whether you removed items from a checklist.


Why IQVIA's Approach Failed Patient codes allowed longitudinal tracking; combined with birth year, sex, diagnoses, prescriptions and location, individuals could be singled out despite removed names and addresses.


Controller vs. Recipient Distinction IQVIA argued it couldn't re-identify patients, but the authority found it was the controller from collection and shaped the anonymization process, so it was judged by what it could do.


Additional GDPR Violations The authority also found no legal basis, no patient notice, no retention limits, no completed data protection impact assessment, and inadequate security with free-text fields leaking identifiers.


Practical Lessons Encryption and pseudonymization are security measures, not anonymization; free-text fields are high-risk; and U.S. HIPAA de-identification standards do not satisfy GDPR requirements.


What Companies Must Do Inventory all datasets called anonymous, apply the three-question test, check free-text fields for leakage, and ensure contracts and notices accurately describe data and controller roles.


FAQs


### What is the difference between HIPAA de-identification and GDPR anonymization?


HIPAA's safe harbor method is a checklist of 18 identifier types to remove, while GDPR applies a three-part test: can anyone using reasonably available means single out, link, or infer facts about a person? Passing HIPAA's list does not mean data is anonymous under GDPR.


### Why wasn't IQVIA's database considered anonymous if it removed names and addresses?


The database kept persistent patient codes that allowed tracking individuals over time, combined with detailed medical histories including diagnoses, prescriptions, birth year, sex and location. This combination allowed individual patients to be singled out and re-identified despite removed direct identifiers.


### Can a company claim data is anonymous for it if someone else holds the re-identification key?


Possibly, but not if the company controlled the anonymization process from the start. IQVIA argued it couldn't access the key, but the authority found it was the controller who shaped collection and anonymization, so it was judged by what it could do, not what it intended.


### Do encryption and pseudonymization make data anonymous?


No. The Italian authority made clear that encryption and pseudonymization are security measures that protect personal data, but they do not turn personal data into anonymous data under GDPR.


### What role did free-text fields play in this case?


Free-text fields in IQVIA's database leaked identifying details for about 3,370 patients, including health data for 3,080. The authority faulted IQVIA for not checking whether such fields contained names, ID numbers or addresses before or after collection.


### What should companies do now if they claim their datasets are anonymous or de-identified?


Inventory all such datasets, apply GDPR's three-question test for singling out, linking and inference, check all free-text fields for leaked identifiers, and ensure contracts and privacy notices accurately describe the data and controller-processor roles.
